source.title: Wrong Before Right: Late Rescue and Interface Failure in Aligned Language Models

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the Hydra effect but studies a different question: whether late-layer contributions rescue internally wrong preferences and whether removing those contributions exposes errors. It does not test whether ablating an attention component causes later components to adapt and compensate.
record.gate_note: The paper reports causal late-layer deprivation and structural-damage results, but these do not measure downstream compensation after ablating an attention layer or head. They are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. The Hydra effect is cited as prior work, not tested.
record.test_reason: The Hydra effect is cited once in related work as prior evidence that late layers overwrite earlier preferences. The experiments attenuate or remove late-layer contributions and track which items flip. No attention layer or head is ablated, and the paper never measures whether later components compensate for an earlier ablation. It neither tests nor uses self-repair, so the relation is cites_only rather than discusses.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it omits three findings. The intact-model wrong-dip predicts which items fail under structural compression but not under quantization. The dip's amplification by alignment depends on the training recipe. A dip-regularized LoRA reduces the causal dip by 67–70% and improves robustness to compression.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses layer-wise difference-in-differences, patchscope-style activation transplantation, and late-layer residual attenuation or structural compression; it does not use an attention-layer or head ablation self-repair comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model family, task family, damage operator, and readout. The paper reports dip-stratified failures under structural damage, but dip-blind quantization failures; natural-language free-generation results are more fragile and can saturate, unlike semantic-candidate readouts.

fits_no_version.finding: Attenuating the last 15% of blocks, dropping late blocks, or late-SVD barely changes aggregate accuracy, but flips concentrate on items with large mid-layer wrong-dips.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late layers correct mid-layer wrong preferences on some items. Removing late contributions exposes those errors selectively. This is late rescue, not compensation for an earlier ablation.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code, stimuli, and artifacts will be released at a public repository and that the arXiv version will be updated with the link.
record.problems: Evidence for the claim’s specific self-repair mechanism is absent. The relevant related experiments concern late-layer deprivation rather than earlier attention-component ablation followed by downstream adaptation. The paper also notes that open-ended free-generation mechanism stratification remains open and that some results are single-seed.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Structural compression and quantization results were not included because they report damage susceptibility or dip-blindness, not compensation after component ablation.

untested.parts: No single attention-layer ablation and no measure of downstream compensation.
No late-MLP erasure measure and no erasure change after an upstream ablation.
No single-head ablations and no measurement on general text.
No compensation measured, so no test of partiality, prompt variance or overcorrection.
No backup heads, copy-suppression heads, LayerNorm rescaling or anti-erasure neurons examined.
No comparison of mean or resample ablation with zero ablation.
No comparison of ablation-based importance scores with direct effects.

record.verdict_notes: The aggregate robustness to late-layer removal (0.98→0.95) might look like redundancy. However, the paper measures no downstream adaptation, so it bears on no version of the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate one attention layer and measure compensatory changes in later attention layers.
Does not measure late-MLP downregulation of the maximum-likelihood token or its change after earlier-component ablation.
Does not ablate single attention heads or measure full-distribution self-repair across general text.
Does not measure variation or overcorrection in compensation following component ablation.
Does not test backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons as mechanisms of ablation self-repair.
Does not compare mean or resample ablations with zero ablation for self-repair.
Does not evaluate ablation-based importance scores against a component's direct effect.
